subject: history
title: The 1973 Oil Shock: One Cut, One Price Jump

questions.prompt: A student says: The 1973 oil crisis pushed prices up because governments printed extra money to pay for dearer oil. What is the best correction?

choices.text: The student is right - prices can only rise across the whole economy if governments print extra money

The price rises started on the supply side, not the money side: the OPEC embargo cut the flow of oil, the world oil price jumped from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, and because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, that one rise was passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices while households cut spending back.
The price rises started with households spending more, which pulled shop prices up first
The embargo raised prices only for petrol, and no other prices changed

questions.misconception: The 1973 oil crisis pushed prices up because governments printed extra money to pay for dearer oil.
questions.explanation: The trap claim is: The 1973 oil crisis pushed prices up because governments printed extra money to pay for dearer oil. In fact The price rises started on the supply side, not the money side: the OPEC embargo cut the flow of oil, the world oil price jumped from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, and because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, that one rise was passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices while households cut spending back.

questions.prompt: After the October 1973 embargo, how did the world oil price move?

choices.text: From about $3 to about $6 a barrel
From about $3 to about $12 a barrel
From about $12 down to about $3 a barrel
It stayed at about $3 a barrel

questions.explanation: Scene 2 works this: the embargo closes the valve on the flow, and with far less oil reaching the market the price bar jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, roughly four times higher.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, state the order in which the oil price rise was passed on after the price jump.
questions.answer: Transport costs rose first, factory costs rose next as dearer transport and energy fed into production, and shop prices rose last as factories passed their higher costs on.
questions.explanation: Scene 3 shows the pass-on directly: one rise carried stage by stage - transport, factories, shops - because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything.

questions.prompt: Explain why household spending fell back after the chain of price rises.
questions.answer: Faced with higher prices for fuel, transport and goods, households could afford less, so they cut spending back and the demand bar fell while prices stayed high.
questions.explanation: Scene 4 shows the end of the chain: the price rises reach households, spending shrinks, and importing economies slow.

questions.prompt: Which list gives the oil-shock chain in order?

choices.text: Embargo cuts the oil flow, world price jumps from about $3 to about $12, transport costs rise, factory costs rise, shop prices rise, households cut spending back
Governments print money, shop prices rise, the oil price jumps, the embargo follows
Households cut spending, shop prices fall, transport costs fall, the oil price jumps
World price jumps, embargo cuts the flow, prices rise only for petrol and nothing else changes

questions.explanation: The whole animation names the chain: one cut, one jump, a chain of higher prices passed on stage by stage, then less spending.
